MIT license and also builds on WASM with a demo running on https://fschutt.github.io/printpdf/

One Google search (yeah I'm old, sorry, nobody "Googles" anymore) for "rust pdf library" shows this. Yet people now redo and redo and redo everything again just to have "their" semi-broken copy of a HTML -> PDF renderer (and then run into the same edge cases that were already fixed before). There are lots of edge cases in typography especially, I recently had a lot of fixes as I was trying to ocr-and-cleanup a 1732 scan of some books with Claude auto-extracting the font. There were a ton of edge cases in the layout, esp. related to column, footnote and sidebar handling, or things like "Hebrew RTL text accidentally disappears if text breaks weirdly", "1-bit image compression", etc.

I have nothing against AI, I use it heavily myself, but what is annoying is people completely ignoring the years of work of existing projects that do the exact same thing - instead of just forking, but instead re-tokenizing the exact same work again. Most likely the author didn't research "does this already exist" and that's annoying, then you get 100 of similar projects reinventing the world with tokens again and again. Sometimes its beneficial and can lead to faster exploration of new approaches, but in most cases its not and misses edge cases that were solved before.

When we evaluated the Rust PDF landscape, printpdf was actually one of the first crates we looked at for PDF generation. The reason we opted for a stack centered around lopdf and pdf-writer was architectural: PaperPilot's primary focus is heavy manipulation and non-destructive AST transformation of existing, arbitrary, often malformed real-world PDFs (re-ordering cross-reference tables, granular /P permission bitmask hashing, raw object streams, page imposition, booklet folding, and outline splitting).

For document synthesis (HTML/Markdown to PDF), typography and edge-cases (like the RTL/footnote issues you mentioned) are notoriously hard, and we'd love to learn from or collaborate with printpdf's battle-tested approaches there. Thank you for the feedback and all your contributions to Rust's PDF ecosystem!

I just ran an security analysis on the repo. As is, it's not looking great (again nothing against vibe/agentic coded projects) the lack of security consideration is astonishing (not suggesting a malice). Definitely NOT production ready.

  Context: about 98% of the commits are by AI bots (Antigravity, Google Jules).
  That explains the bugs below.

  Security bugs

  1. High: the local web API lets any website use the user's files.
  - paperpilot-gateway/src/server.rs:95-98 allows requests from any website, and
    there's no login or authentication.
  - POST /api/v1/pdf/mcp-exec (handlers.rs:233) runs any tool with any file path
    on the machine.
  - So while the API is running, any web page the user visits can make it
    overwrite files with PDFs, create folders, and read back text from any local
    PDF.
  - In the desktop app the user has to switch the API on. But docker-compose.yml
    opens it to the network with no authentication.
  - There's also no limit on request size (usize::MAX), so one huge request can
    exhaust memory.

  2. High: a malicious document can run code in the desktop app.
  - Search results display text from the user's own documents as raw HTML
    without escaping it:
    - WorkspaceSearchModal.svelte:297
    - workspaceSearch.ts:84
    - WorkspaceSearchModal.svelte:118
  - The app has no Content Security Policy, and lets its window read any file on
    disk (tauri.conf.json:28-33, scope "**").
  - So a PDF or DOCX carrying an  payload could read any local
    file and send it out once the user searches it.

  3. Medium: downloaded models and add-on packs are never verified.
  - There's no checksum check on models (ai_commands.rs, ocr_commands.rs). Some
    come straight from the repo's live main branch, so whatever lands there
    ships to users.
  - Pack downloads (pack_commands.rs:147-151) put pack_id straight into the file
    path. A value containing ../ writes outside the app's data folder.
  - Packs come from huggingface.co/paperpilot/packs, an account I didn't confirm
    the project owns.

  4. Medium/Low: the protection against fetching internal addresses can be
  bypassed (paperpilot-core/src/url_fetch.rs:24-40).
  - It only checks IP addresses typed directly into the URL, not what a domain
    name resolves to.
  - It follows redirects, so a public URL can redirect to an internal one.
  - IPv6 addresses ([::1]), 0.0.0.0 and the 100.64.0.0/10 range get through.
  - The impact is limited because the response must start with %PDF.

  5. Low: CI supply chain.
  - release.yml installs wasm-pack via curl | sh.
  - GitHub Actions are pinned to version tags, not commit hashes.
  - The Android build ignores the lockfile (--no-frozen-lockfile).

In case you don't have showdead on, the OP writes:

""" I built PaperPilot because I was frustrated by the privacy trade-offs of modern PDF utilities.

Whenever you need to split, merge, compress, or sign a confidential document (tax forms, legal contracts, medical paperwork) using online tools, your files are transmitted to a third-party server. Most "free" tools retain copies or run in closed-source cloud environments.

PaperPilot is a 100% zero-cloud, local-first engine written in pure Rust (built on top of lopdf, pdf-writer, and image). 0 bytes are ever sent to an external server.

Key aspects of the project:

1. Penta-Interface Architecture: Instead of building just another web app or CLI, the same core Rust operations run across 5 surfaces: - Terminal CLI: High-throughput local processing and bash scripting. - Local Desktop App: Native cross-platform GUI built with Tauri 2 and Svelte 5. - Client-Side Web: Runs 100% inside your browser via WebAssembly (https://usepaperpilot.com/). - REST / Gateway API: Standalone local daemon (localhost:7823) for local microservices. - Model Context Protocol (MCP): Connects local AI agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, OpenCode) directly to local PDF tools so LLMs can inspect, redact, and sign PDFs on disk without cloud upload.

2. Capabilities (75+ Tools): - Standard operations: Merge, split, rotate, reorder, burst, booklet imposition, and N-up grid. - Privacy & Compliance: Local PII regex redaction (SSNs, cards, emails), metadata striping, and digital signature verification. - Document Extraction: PDF to structured Markdown tables (no coordinate loss), PDF to JSON, and pure-Rust layout analysis. - Offline RAG: Embedded vector store (libsql_vector) with an actionable visual citation canvas.

3. Performance & License: - Average operation latency is ~20ms to 130ms. - 100% Free and Open Source under the Apache 2.0 license.

The GitHub repository is at https://github.com/KrushnaVardhanReddy/PaperPilot and the browser-based WASM sandbox is live at https://usepaperpilot.com/.

I’d love to hear your feedback on the architecture, performance benchmarks, and any edge-case PDF formats we should test against! """
